chapter_theme: Kemasari, waking to find that Civakan has left her in the night, laments to him, to the creatures and places around her, to her own eyes, shoulders, breasts and reflection; understanding at last the veiled words he spoke to the bee, she holds back her life for fear of harm to him and takes the bees as household gods, while a companion asks the house deity whether she can survive, and the morning star rises.

cast.role: the merchant's daughter Civakan married and has left in the night
one of Kemasari's household, likely her companion, who speaks to the house deity (unnamed)
the bees of her garland, of which Civakan spoke before he left
Kemasari's own reflection, which she takes for a weeping friend
the creatures, places and her own limbs that she addresses in her lament

1509.reading: Finding him gone, Kemasari cries out asking where her lord is, says she is afraid because her dear life strains to quit her body, confesses she has no restraint left, and begs the long-armed one to come back to her.
1509.nuance: நிறையான் இலேன், 'I have no nirai', is her own admission that the self-containment a woman is meant to keep has gone; the narrator still calls her speech honey-sweet (தேனின் மிழற்றினாள்).
1509.event: Kemasari wakes, finds Civakan gone, and calls out to him.

1510.reading: She throws back at him his own saying that women are sweetest when ripe love mingles and two lives become one, and asks whether it is fitting that she, pale as the dewy moon, should now be alone.
1510.nuance: Her argument turns his own doctrine of love, that the lovers' lives become one, into the charge against him: if their lives are one, his leaving her alone contradicts what he taught.
1510.event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

1511.reading: Her heart slipping, her bangles loosening, her eyes wheeling and her body burning like heated gold, she says she cannot bear it and asks whether he has cast off even the love that should be as hard to shed as one's shadow.
1511.nuance: The simile நிழலின் நீப்பருங் காதல், love as inseparable as a shadow, is taken up literally in 1524 and 1525, where the only thing that stays with her is her own reflection.
1511.event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

1512.reading: She calls him a deceiver who used to say that her slender waist suffered even under a jasmine garland, and asks whether he can now bear to see her scorched.
1512.nuance: வஞ்ச நீ is the first time she names him a deceiver; his remembered tenderness is offered as evidence against him.
1512.event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

1513.reading: She recalls how he praised her coral lips and breasts, saying the gods would melt to see them, and says she did not grasp the meaning of what was said about the bee, he of the honey-dripping garland.
1513.nuance: Line 3 looks back to 1501 and 1502, where Civakan, about to leave in the night, spoke to the bee on her garland of a bee whose mate stays on without grief; she now sees the words were a covert notice of his going. வண்டு கூறிய can be 'what the bee said' or 'what was said of (to) the bee'.
1513.event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

1514.reading: She recalls that if a thorn so much as touched her on the way he would bow his head to the ground and stroke her foot, says she is bewildered, and asks the master of the bow, the guardian of her life who has now shaken it, for grace.
1514.nuance: She calls him என் உயிர் காவலனே, guardian of my life, in the same line that says he has shaken that life (உலைவித்தனை).
1514.event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

1515.reading: She recalls him painting designs over every part of her pearl-strung breasts and living as one with her, and says that for one who cannot follow him, living on is mere folly.
1515.nuance: Line 3 (உழைவார் அலனேன்) is hard to divide; the sense 'I am not one who can go where you are' is the likeliest but not certain.
1515.event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

1516.reading: Because he had said she was one who would always have love, and no one had said her love would be cut off, she asks him to pity her as she wastes to the bone and to come near.
1516.nuance: The verse plays பெறும் அன்பினள், she who receives love, against அறும் அன்பினள், she whose love is severed.
1516.event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

1517.reading: She quotes his words, 'if you walk your small feet will ache; you live within my life', tells him that he lied, and says he has gone alone and left her, the one of evil deeds.
1517.nuance: வினையேன், 'I of (bad) deeds', is the usual self-name of one in grief, but it places a cause in her own past deeds in the same breath as she calls his word a lie (பொய்யுரைத்தனை): she blames both.
1517.event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

1518.reading: She says that, torn from his pearl-hung chest before her breasts had had their fill of it, she has been given two burnings, the blaze of desire and the burning of a spear wound in the breast.
1518.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are obscure as divided; the two fires may be desire and grief rather than any literal wound.
1518.event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

1519.reading: She calls on the peacock of the field, the grove, the stream, the plantain, the hill and the waves, says she worships them, and asks whether through them she may find again the man of the fiery jewels.
1519.event: Kemasari appeals to the creatures and places around her to help her find Civakan.

1520.reading: She says her pain, crueller than an arrow, grows at midnight, the chariot of the long white moonlight does not move on, and she asks Virtue standing on the way to show her grace.
1520.nuance: அறனே அருளாய் addresses Aram itself as a power that could end the night; she appeals not to a god but to virtue, which she implies her desertion has offended.
1520.event: Kemasari, sleepless at midnight, appeals to Virtue.

1521.reading: Turning to her flower-like eyes, which he once likened to kayal fish, she says that all he said of her innocence has come to nothing and asks them to tell her how she may survive.
1521.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard to divide (கவிழ்ந்து கிடந்து, அயலேன் அறியாமை); the reading of what he said of her is not secure.
1521.event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

1522.reading: She asks her shoulders, on which he painted bangles and pearls and which he praised, which way the fragrant-garlanded one went, since they must know.
1522.event: Kemasari questions her own shoulders about where Civakan went.

1523.reading: She asks her breasts, which ploughed the chest of the young man of the bright spear, why they did not follow the bull when it left the diamond stall, and the jewelled one weeps.
1523.nuance: Civakan is the bull (விடை) leaving its stall; the image makes his going a matter of nature as much as of fault.
1523.event: Kemasari reproaches her breasts and weeps.

1524.reading: Seeing her own reflection, its beauty wasted, shedding tears and weeping, she tells it not to grieve and not to weep, her dear friend, asking whether he could ever be an enemy.
1524.nuance: She gives her image the consolation a friend would give her: அவரோ பகையாபவர், 'would he turn enemy?'. The hope she cannot hold for herself she offers to her reflection.
1524.event: Kemasari takes her reflection for a weeping companion and comforts it.

1525.reading: When the fallen garlands covered the floor and she could no longer see her reflection, she thought it had gone to search out the way he took, and waited long, saying it would come back now.
1525.nuance: Line 4 (எறிவால் வளை கொண்டு வரும்) is obscure; it may say the reflection will come back bringing him, or her bangles.
1525.event: Kemasari loses sight of her reflection under the fallen garlands and waits for it to return.

1526.reading: She calls on the peahen, the cuckoo, the stately swan and the parrot who played with her, melting as she calls them her own, until her speech, sweet as the yazh, fails.
1526.nuance: எனை அனை may be 'like me' or 'my mother'; either way she treats the birds as kin.
1526.event: Kemasari calls on her pet birds until her voice fails.

1527.reading: As the woman, fallen into the fire of separation from the garlanded warrior, lies burnt, one of her household looks to the deity of the house and speaks in pity.
1527.nuance: The verse does not name who speaks to the house deity (இல்லுறை தெய்வம்); a companion is the likeliest, and the speech follows in 1528 and 1529.
1527.event: While Kemasari lies spent, someone of her household turns to the house deity and speaks.

1528.reading: The speaker asks the house deity whether, when even Kama seeing the warrior's beauty would long to become a woman, this doe-like girl can survive.
1528.nuance: பெண் அவா நிற்கும்: Kama himself would long to be a woman for Civakan's sake, a hyperbole that makes her grief beyond blame.

1529.reading: The speaker asks whether a young cow elephant can live when the rutting bull who fed her honeyed morsels with his trunk has left her, and so whether the garlanded girl can live now that the generous-handed one has gone.

1530.reading: The narrator says that, taking the bee as the one her lover had spoken of, the woman turned to the deity and, understanding, fearing both harm to her husband and their parting, held back the life that was leaving her.
1530.nuance: She lives on for fear of harm (ஊனம்) to her husband, not only in hope of his return; the narrator hedges with என்ப போலும். முகிழ்முலைத் தெய்வம் சேர is hard to construe.
1530.event: Kemasari understands Civakan's words about the bee and resolves to live.

1531.reading: She tells all to see the gem-coloured bee that the deceiving Kama spoke of, and asks the bees to be gods worthy of worship in her golden mansion so that her grief may end.
1531.nuance: She calls Civakan காமன் and his mouth deceitful (வஞ்சவாய்), yet makes the bee he addressed an object of worship.
1531.event: Kemasari takes the bees as household gods.

1532.reading: The girl, so frail that a ball was too heavy for her, wasted like a butter doll left in the sun, and the morning star rose in the sky like a jewel on its brow.
1532.event: As Kemasari wastes, the morning star rises and the night ends.

links.note: She now says she did not grasp the words about the bee that Civakan spoke before he left.
links.teaches: Read together, the bee speech that sounds like idle love-play in 1502 proves to be his only farewell, and her failure to decode it becomes part of her grief.

links.note: She holds back her life on the strength of the bee words, in which the mate stays on without grief when the other goes.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the covert message doing its work: the image of the mate who waits without grieving, left in place of a goodbye, becomes the rule by which she chooses to live.

links.note: The life she says in 1509 is leaving her body is held back in 1530.
links.teaches: The two verses frame the lament between a life about to go and a life restrained, and show that what turns it is not his return but her fear of harm to him.

links.note: Love said to cling like a shadow in 1511; her actual reflection taken for a companion in 1524.
links.teaches: The love she said should cling like a shadow has gone, and what stays is her literal image, which she then comforts as a friend, so the simile becomes her situation.

links.note: Both are a deserted woman weighing the assurance of the man who left.
links.teaches: The couplet asks whether those who trusted an assurance are at fault, and the epic heroine answers both ways at once, calling his word a lie and naming herself the one of evil deeds.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's moral question, so her cry that he lied reads as a judgment on who answers for a broken assurance
gains.b: the couplet gains the promise in its exact words and a speaker who does not acquit herself, which it never shows

links.note: Both make the woman's shoulders the record of union and parting.
links.teaches: In the couplet the shoulders betray the parting to onlookers, while the epic woman questions her shoulders as witnesses of where he went, so the body that tells the secret becomes a confidant.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the convention that the shoulders bear the sign of union and parting, which explains why she turns to them
gains.b: the couplet gains a reason the shoulders should know: he painted them, and they are asked rather than read

links.note: Both put the parted woman at night with no companion but herself.
links.teaches: The couplet's woman mocks the night for having only her as companion, and the epic's woman, as alone, makes her own reflection the companion and consoles it, so the loneliness turns inward on the self.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the Kural's frame of the night that has no companion, which shows her talking to her image is the extreme of that solitude
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene where the absence of any companion is acted out, not stated

links.note: The companion appeals to the deity that dwells in the house; Kemasari then installs the bees as the gods of her house.
links.teaches: The house god that the household turns to for her survival is answered by her own choice of new household gods, the bees of his parting words, so worship shifts from the family's deity to the creature his parting words named.

source_issues: 1527-1532: printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the build.
1531 line 1: வங்சவாய்க் is very likely a misprint for வஞ்சவாய்க்.
1514 line 1, 1515 line 3, 1518 lines 3-4, 1521 lines 1-2, 1525 line 4: word division in the edition is unclear and the sense is uncertain.
1530 line 1: முகிழ்முலைத் தெய்வஞ் சேர is hard to construe.
